title: How to order equipment
summary: The four steps from a doctor's prescription to equipment set up in your home.
body:
Most medical equipment needs a prescription and some paperwork before your insurance will pay for it. We handle most of that for you. Here is what happens.

1. Your doctor sends an order

Ask your doctor or discharge planner to send us an order. It should name the equipment, explain why you need it and include notes from a recent visit. Prescribers can fax or send it electronically.

2. We check your coverage

We confirm your benefits with your plan, ask for any prior authorization and call you with what you will owe before anything is delivered.

3. We deliver and set up

A technician or respiratory therapist brings the equipment, sets it up and shows you and your caregivers how to use it. Most deliveries happen within one or two business days.

4. We stay in touch

We call after the first week, handle refills and resupply, and repair or replace equipment that stops working.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Medicare and your equipment
summary: What Medicare Part B covers, what you pay, and how rentals work.
body:
Medicare Part B covers durable medical equipment that your doctor prescribes for use in your home.

What you pay

After you meet the yearly Part B deductible, you usually pay 20 percent of the Medicare-approved amount. A supplemental or Medicare Advantage plan may pay some or all of that.

Rent or own

Many items are capped rentals. Medicare pays a monthly rental, and after 13 continuous months the equipment becomes yours. Oxygen equipment is rented for 36 months, after which your supplier keeps providing it and servicing it for up to five years in total.

What Medicare does not cover

Items mainly for comfort or convenience, such as shower chairs and grab bars, are usually not covered. Many are HSA and FSA eligible.

We are a Medicare-enrolled supplier and accept assignment, which means we accept the Medicare-approved amount as full payment.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Cleaning and caring for your CPAP
summary: A simple daily and weekly routine that keeps therapy comfortable and your equipment lasting.
body:
Clean equipment is more comfortable and lasts longer.

Every day

  • Empty the humidifier and let it air dry
  • Wipe the mask cushion with a mask wipe or mild soap and water

Every week

  • Wash the mask, tubing and humidifier chamber in warm soapy water, rinse and air dry out of sunlight
  • Check the filter and replace it if it looks dirty

Replacement supplies

Most plans cover new cushions, masks, tubing and filters on a regular schedule. We can remind you and ship them automatically.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: What your doctor needs to send us
summary: The details an order needs so your insurance approves it the first time.
body:
Insurance plans are strict about paperwork. Missing details are the most common reason an order is delayed.

A complete order includes

  • Your full name, date of birth and insurance details
  • The equipment, including any accessories, and how long you need it
  • Your diagnosis and why the equipment is medically necessary
  • Notes from a visit in the last six months that describe your condition
  • Your doctor's signature and the date

Extra items for some equipment

  • Oxygen: a recent oxygen test result
  • CPAP: the sleep study report
  • Hospital beds: why a regular bed will not work

If anything is missing, we contact your doctor's office directly, so you do not have to.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Choosing a walker or rollator
summary: Standard walkers, two-wheel walkers and rollators: which one fits how you move.
body:
The right walker depends on how much support you need and where you will use it.

Standard walker

The most stable choice. You lift it with each step, so it suits people who need a lot of support for short distances.

Two-wheel walker

Front wheels let you push instead of lift. A good middle ground after surgery.

Rollator

Four wheels, hand brakes and a seat. Best for people who can walk longer distances but need to rest along the way. It needs good grip strength to use the brakes.

Getting the height right

Stand up straight with your arms relaxed. The handles should line up with the crease of your wrist. We set this for you at delivery.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Understanding your bill
summary: Deductibles, coinsurance and rental statements, explained in plain language.
body:
Equipment bills can look different from doctor bills, especially for rentals.

Monthly rental statements

For rented equipment you get a statement each month while the rental continues. The amount should be the same each month unless your plan or deductible changes.

Words you will see

  • Deductible: what you pay each year before your plan starts paying
  • Coinsurance: your share after the deductible, often 20 percent
  • Allowed amount: the price your plan has agreed to pay

Paying your bill

We do not take payments on this website. Call our billing team to pay by phone, set up a payment plan or ask about financial assistance.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Getting your home ready for a hospital bed
summary: Measure, clear a path and plan where the bed goes before delivery day.
body:
A little planning makes delivery quick and keeps everyone safe.

Before we arrive

  • Choose a room on the main floor if you can, close to a bathroom
  • Leave at least three feet of space on both sides of the bed for caregivers
  • Clear a path at least 36 inches wide from the door
  • Make sure there is a grounded outlet within reach

On delivery day

Our technicians assemble the bed, test every function and show you how to raise the head, lower the rails and lock the wheels.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.

title: Oxygen safety at home
summary: Simple rules for using oxygen safely around the house.
body:
Oxygen is safe when used correctly, but it makes fires burn faster and hotter.

Do

  • Keep oxygen at least ten feet from open flames, gas stoves and candles
  • Put up a no smoking sign and make sure smoke alarms work
  • Store spare cylinders upright in a stand, away from heat

Do not

  • Never smoke or let anyone smoke near you while oxygen is in use
  • Do not use oil-based lotions or petroleum jelly on your face
  • Do not change your flow setting without talking to your doctor

If your concentrator alarms or stops working, switch to a backup cylinder and call our 24-hour respiratory line.

This guide is general information to help you prepare. It is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor about what is right for you.
